name: Ibn Battuta
info: Ibn Battuta was a Maghrebi Muslim traveller and scholar from Tangier who between 1325 and 1354 visited much of Africa, Asia and the Iberian Peninsula, and is remembered for the account of his journeys known as the Rihla.

facts.born: 24 February 1304, in Tangier under the Marinid dynasty; of Arabised Berber descent, from the Lawata clan and a family of Islamic legal scholars
facts.died: 1368 or 1369, in Morocco, where he had been appointed a judge; little is known of his last years
facts.role: Traveller and scholar; qadi (judge) under Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq in Delhi; chief qadi in the Maldives; envoy charged with the Delhi Sultanate's embassy to Yuan China (from 1341); judge in Morocco after 1354
facts.known: Travels of around 117,000 km over about thirty years; four pilgrimages to Mecca; service as a judge in Delhi and the Maldives; journeys to China, the Swahili coast and the Mali Empire; The Rihla, dictated to Ibn Juzayy; doubts over how much of it he saw himself

t: Ibn Battuta left Tangier in 1325 to make the pilgrimage to Mecca and did not return to Morocco for 24 years, travelling through the Middle East, East Africa, Anatolia, Central Asia, India, Southeast Asia and China.
He lived by his learning in Islamic law, serving as a judge in Delhi and the Maldives, and grew wealthy on the gifts of rulers, among them the slaves he was given and bought.

His account of the journeys, dictated to Ibn Juzayy after 1354, is the only source for his life; scholars have shown that parts of it were copied from earlier travellers and doubt that he saw every place he describes.
dyk: The patronymic Ibn Battuta literally means 'son of a duckling'; in the Rihla he gives his full name as Shams al-Din Abu 'Abdallah Muhammad ibn 'Abdallah ibn Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf Lawati al-Tanji ibn Battuta.
ev: Ibn Battuta is born in Tangier, into a family of Islamic legal scholars
He sets out from Tangier, aged 21, on the pilgrimage to Mecca
He completes his first pilgrimage at Mecca and decides to travel on to the Ilkhanate
He and his party reach the Indus, and in Delhi Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq appoints him a qadi
He is given charge of an embassy to the Yuan dynasty of China and leaves Delhi
He reaches Quanzhou in China, then under the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty
He crosses the Sahara with a caravan to the Mali Empire
He returns to Morocco and dictates the account of his travels to Ibn Juzayy

sections.early:
All that is known of Ibn Battuta's life comes from the account of his travels. It records that he was of Arabised Berber descent, born in Tangier on 24 February 1304, during the reign of the Marinid dynasty, into a family of Islamic legal scholars, known in the Muslim traditions of Morocco as qadis. His family belonged to a Berber tribal clan, the Lawata. His most common full name is given as Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Battuta, a patronymic meaning 'son of a duckling'.

As a young man he would have studied at a Sunni Maliki school, the dominant form of education in North Africa at the time, and that training in law was to be his living abroad: Maliki Muslims elsewhere asked him to serve as their religious judge because he came from a land where their school was practised.

On 2 Rajab 725 AH, 14 June 1325, he left his home town at the age of 21 to make the hajj to Mecca, a journey that would ordinarily take sixteen months. He was, by his own account, eager to learn about far-away lands. He set out alone, he wrote, "swayed by an overmastering impulse within me", and grieved at leaving his parents, both still living. He would not see Morocco again for 24 years.
sections.rise:
He went overland along the North African coast, through Tlemcen, Béjaïa and Tunis, usually joining a caravan for safety, and in Sfax took the first of the many wives of his travels. In the early spring of 1326 he reached Alexandria in the Bahri Mamluk realm, where, by his account, the ascetic Sheikh Burhanuddin foretold that he would travel to India and China. From Cairo a rebellion turned him back from the Red Sea, and he went instead through Damascus and Medina to Mecca, completing his first pilgrimage in November 1326 and taking the honorific El-Hajji.

Rather than return home, he travelled on: through Iraq and Iran to Baghdad, where he joined for a while the caravan of Abu Sa'id, the last Mongol ruler of the unified Ilkhanate, then to Tabriz and Mosul. He stayed in Mecca for a time, perhaps three years, though problems of chronology lead commentators to suggest he left after the 1328 hajj. He sailed down the Red Sea to Yemen and Aden, then along the coast of Somalia to Mogadishu and down the Swahili coast to Kilwa, whose ruler he praised. In the autumn of 1330 or 1332 he set out to seek employment with Muhammad bin Tughluq, Sultan of Delhi, by way of Anatolia, the Golden Horde and Constantinople, Bukhara and Samarkand, and the Hindu Kush. His party reached the Indus on 12 September 1333.
sections.deeds:
In Delhi the sultan, renowned as the wealthiest man in the Muslim world, appointed him a qadi on the strength of his years of study in Mecca. For six years he veered between the high life of a trusted subordinate and suspicion of treason. In 1341 he was given charge of an embassy to the Yuan dynasty of China; on the way bandits robbed and nearly killed him, and at Calicut a storm sank one of the expedition's ships while the other sailed without him. Afraid to return to Delhi a failure, he stayed in southern India and then went to the Maldives.

There he spent nine months as chief judge, married into the royal family of Omar I and took four wives. He tried to bring local practice closer to a strict application of Muslim law, ordering that men who missed Friday prayer be publicly whipped and that robbers' right hands be cut off, until his judgements set the rulers against him and he resigned. By way of Sri Lanka, the Madurai Sultanate and Chittagong, where in 1345 he met the Sufi Shah Jalal, he sailed to Samudra Pasai in Sumatra and on to Quanzhou in China in 1345. He described its silk, porcelain and paper money, went on to Guangzhou, Fuzhou and Hangzhou, and says he reached the Yuan court of Emperor Huizong at Beijing.
sections.opponents:
The Rihla records the slavery that ran through his travels. In Anatolia the ruler of the Beylik of Aydin gave him his first slave; he bought a young Greek girl for 40 dinars in Ephesus and was given and bought others. He insulted Greeks as "enemies of Allah", drunkards and "swine eaters" while keeping a Greek girl among the slave girls of his "harem". He took wives wherever he stayed and divorced them when he moved on, had children by wives or concubines in several cities, and waited two decades to learn what had become of a wife and child in Damascus. In Mali he wrote that black Africans were characterised by "ill manners" and that he "was long astonished at their feeble intellect"; he left the Sahara with a caravan carrying 600 female slaves.

The account itself has long been questioned. He seems to have kept no notes, and Ibn Juzayy copied passages from Ibn Jubayr, writing more than 150 years earlier, and from Muhammad al-Abdari without saying so. Modern scholars doubt that he visited every place described: a trip up the Volga to Bolghar is thought very unlikely, and his journeys to Sanaa and around Anatolia are in doubt. Some question whether he reached China, where his account shares material with Shihab al-Umari and others and confuses the Yellow River with the Grand Canal. Henry Yule and William Henry Scott thought the princess Urduja and her land of Tawalisi entirely fictitious, and the German scholar Ralph Elger suspects much of the work to be a fiction compiled from other travel reports.
sections.last:
He left Quanzhou in 1346 and began the journey home. In the Strait of Hormuz he learned that Abu Sa'id had died and his lands had collapsed into civil war. In 1348 he reached Damascus, where he learned that his father had died fifteen years before, and he travelled on through the Black Death: the toll in Damascus, he heard, reached 2,400 a day, Gaza was depopulated and deaths in Cairo were reported at 1,100 a day. After a last hajj he came back to Tangier by way of Fez in 1349, to find that his mother too had died a few months earlier.

In 1350 he joined Muslims going to defend Gibraltar against Alfonso XI of Castile, but the plague had killed the king and he toured al-Andalus as far as Granada instead. In February 1352 he left Sijilmasa with a caravan across the Sahara, by the salt mines of Taghaza and Oualata, to the capital of the Mali Empire, where he met Mansa Suleyman, and went on by Timbuktu to Gao. In the desert a message from the Sultan of Morocco commanded him home, and he returned early in 1354.

At the suggestion of the Marinid ruler Abu Inan Faris he dictated an account of his journeys to the scholar Ibn Juzayy, completed in 1355. Little is known of his life after that. He was appointed a judge in Morocco and died in 1368 or 1369.
sections.legacy:
The Rihla, whose full title may be translated as A Masterpiece to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities and the Marvels of Travelling, was unknown outside the Muslim world until the early 19th century. Ulrich Jasper Seetzen acquired an abridged manuscript in the Middle East, Johann Kosegarten published extracts in 1818, and Samuel Lee's English translation of another abridgement appeared in London in 1829. In the 1830s, during the French occupation of Algeria, the Bibliothèque Nationale acquired five manuscripts, one dated 1356 and believed to be Ibn Juzayy's autograph, from which Charles Defrémery and Beniamino Sanguinetti published from 1853 the Arabic text with a French translation. Hamilton Gibb's English translation for the Hakluyt Society was completed by Charles Beckingham in 1994.

Even if it is not fully based on what its author witnessed, the Rihla provides an important account of much of the 14th-century world, and his itinerary shows scholars when Islam first began to spread into the heart of West Africa. It holds the earliest mention of the Mande xylophone. By its reckoning he travelled around 117,000 km, more than any other explorer in pre-modern history. In 1987 Ross E. Dunn doubted that evidence would be found to support the narrative, but in 2010 Tim Mackintosh-Smith reported manuscripts of Islamic law copied by Ibn Battuta in Damascus in 1326, which bear out the Rihla's date. Tangier's airport and a mall in Dubai bear his name.

summary: Ibn Battuta, born in Tangier in 1304, left on the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1325 and travelled for nearly thirty years across Africa, Asia and al-Andalus, serving as a judge in Delhi and the Maldives. The Rihla he dictated after 1354 is the only source for his life, and scholars doubt that he saw all he describes.

notes: Death: the article gives '1368 or 1369'; I set end 1368 with endCirca true.

Chronology: the article gives alternative years for much of 1328-1334 (the hajj of 1328 or 1330, Aden 1329 or 1331, the start for Anatolia 1330 or 1332, Constantinople 1332 or 1334). It also dates the Kilwa visit to 1330 and the Mogadishu arrival to 1332, which do not fit together; I gave no year for either.
'Says he reached the Yuan court': the article narrates the Beijing visit flatly but also reports that some scholars question whether he visited China at all; I hedged the court visit only.
Where the article says 'it is said' or 'by his account' (Burhanuddin's prophecy), I kept the attribution to the Rihla.
The 117,000 km figure is the lead's, unattributed; I tied it to the Rihla's reckoning, since the article says the Rihla is the only source for his journeys.
The Black Death figures are those he reported ('he heard', 'reportedly'), not counts.

The 'opponents' section: the article names no personal opponents beyond the Maldivian rulers his judgements antagonised and the Delhi sultan's suspicion; I filled it with the slavery and remarks the article records and with the scholarly doubts about the Rihla, all attributed as the article gives them.

Wanted but not in the article: where and how he died; his family in later life; the names of his wives; details of his office as a judge in Morocco; how he returned from Beijing beyond the bare route; Ibn Juzayy's dates.
